extracted.intended_audience: marketers, brand managers, packaging designers, product designers, and creatives working on consumer-packaged-goods rebrands
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for redesigning or judging packaging and brand rebrands for everyday consumer products (example: juice carton). Focuses on legibility, recognizability, information hierarchy, shelf performance, and research/testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and rapid communication of key product information
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you convey the right information to your customer and do it quickly. Consumer choices are split-second decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the most important product information its own, clearly marked space (example: old design had a big red box for 'No pulp'). Avoid burying essential facts inside decorative artwork (e.g., putting 'Pulp Free' in red inside an illustrated glass). Design must allow instant recognition of the product attributes without time-consuming inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility at normal viewing distance and orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Packaging text and logos must be easy to read when customers view products at typical shelf distances and angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thin fonts, low contrast, or unusual orientations (the article criticizes the post-rebrand vertical, thin logo that forces customers to tilt their heads). Ensure font weight, color contrast, and placement support immediate reading from three feet away; don’t force customers to assume odd viewing postures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve distinctive/iconic brand elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep characteristic, memorable brand visuals that customers already associate with the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing a recognizable mark (example: Tropicana's orange-with-straw) can destroy established customer-brand relationships and make shoppers unable to find the product. If the brand’s strength is standing out, avoid redesigns that make it blend in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function over abstract symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful or conceptual symbolism must not come at the expense of basic functionality and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that prioritize esoteric ideas ('love', 'modern') over clarity lead to confusion. The article calls out Arnell's dreamlike symbolism and jargon as signs the designers were 'out there'—an anti-pattern for commodity products where practicality matters most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shelf-context performance and grouping robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs must work when cartons are displayed in realistic, clustered shelf contexts rather than as isolated, perfectly-angled mockups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid visuals that rely on a single-carton perspective (e.g., putting a glass image 'across two sides' that only aligns from a precise angle). Test how a packed shelf looks; most shoppers see clustered products, not perfectly positioned single units.

rubrics_metrics.name: High contrast and accessible color choices for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use color and contrast combinations that ensure text and labels are readable against their backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites white font on yellow as weaker contrast compared to dark green on white. Avoid placing important text inside visually complex areas (like inside an illustration of juice) where it can be 'hidden in plain sight.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear depiction of the product (unambiguous symbolism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use straightforward visual cues that clearly signal what the product is and what it contains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing the fruit (orange) gave instant meaning; vague symbols like yellow liquid in a cocktail glass created ambiguity (did it suggest mixed drinks?). For everyday consumables, literal, unambiguous imagery often performs better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness: packaging must stand out among competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: A rebrand should not cause the product to disappear into the mass of similar-looking competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the previous packaging occupied a unique visual niche, avoid switching to a bland, 'average-joe' design that makes the product indistinguishable on shelf. Distinctive cues maintain customer recognition and loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing extra effort or embarrassment on customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices should not require customers to take awkward actions or feel foolish to use/recognize the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vertical logo that forces head-tilt. Such friction discourages purchase and harms brand experience. User ergonomics and ease of comprehension are part of good design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative balance between information and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design is a back-and-forth process: information → presentation → information until both beauty and functionality are achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize securing a proper flow of product data first, then refine visual effects. Iterate with stakeholders and users to settle on a solution that's both attractive and usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test with real customers early and simply
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate packaging concepts with actual consumers using even simple graphics or mockups to reveal likely problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues Arnell likely never showed simple mockups to consumers; a basic test would have surfaced broad disapproval. Use quick, inexpensive tests (e.g., simple shelf mockups, preference tests) to catch fatal flaws before launch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not blindly follow trends; respect brand positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid redesigns that chase 'modern' or mainstream aesthetics if the brand's position is to stand out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jargon like 'bring the brand to a more current or modern state' can mask a design that simply fits in. If your brand equity derives from standing out, redesigns should reinforce—not dilute—that positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to small functional innovations but not at expense of core clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactile or ergonomic details (e.g., a squeeze cap modeled on an orange) can be valuable enhancements, but they shouldn't substitute for essential visual and informational clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article praises Tropicana’s new haptic cap as a useful touch and notes the company kept that feature after reverting the packaging, but warns that such niceties don't justify fundamentally flawed visual changes that harm sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empower internal stakeholders to call out obvious problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage team members to speak up when a design 'looks wrong' rather than deferring to jargon or prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece stresses raising a hand and saying 'Wait a minute! That just looks wrong.' Organizational candor and simple common-sense objections can prevent costly launches.
